Clinical Compass

A traceable, patient-facing guide from diagnosis to doctor-visit questions

Clinical Compass turns a new diagnosis into plain language, source-backed treatment context, safer questions, and clickable recruiting US trials.

Yale SOM · MGT 409: AI Foundations for Managers Emma Holub
The promise is practical: help a person ask a better question and participate in a shared treatment decision. It informs the conversation; it does not diagnose or prescribe.

Live app  ·  Public GitHub repository

This is a patient preparation tool, not a replacement for care. The product organizes reliable evidence so a person can use a short appointment more effectively. Its most important design boundary is that the clinician still diagnoses, recommends, and decides with the patient.
The problem · who has it

Patients leave the room without what they need

A new diagnosis creates an information problem at the exact moment a visit is too short to solve it. The audience is broad: patients, parents, and caregivers who need a readable starting point before the next decision.

The opportunity is practical: turn confusion into specific, source-backed questions before the next appointment. That could be life-changing in a serious case, but the product must earn that claim through testing.

These figures describe the problem space, not Clinical Compass’s measured impact; each source is linked so the audience can inspect the population and study context.

Patients may delay care, stop treatment, or leave the most important question unasked when they do not understand a treatment plan. The three figures establish why orientation matters, but they do not claim Clinical Compass caused those outcomes. The product hypothesis is that a prepared patient can use the next conversation more safely and productively.
What's new · competitive landscape

Not a search engine. Not a chatbot. Not alone, either.

WhoWhat they doWhere Clinical Compass differs

The point is shared decision-making: make evidence, tradeoffs, questions, and legitimate trial options visible enough for a patient to discuss them.

Control test (October 24): asked the same question, ChatGPT gave a careful answer but no drug-specific numbers, no exact quote behind any claim, and one trial (Phase 1, 40 people) that Compass’s filters exclude.
Control test: I asked ChatGPT, logged out, the same rheumatoid arthritis question on October 24. Its answer was careful and accurate as far as I could check, and it declined to invent discontinuation rates. But it gave no drug-specific numbers at all, including the leflunomide response rate printed on the FDA label, cited per paragraph rather than per claim, and listed a Phase 1 study of 40 people among its trials. The full transcript is in the repo. I also deliberately did not fake a prescribing-volume ranking from data I do not have a license to use. The competitive question is not whether ChatGPT or OpenEvidence can produce a medical paragraph. They can. The difference is the bounded artifact: named public sources, evidence attached to each treatment, safety separated from efficacy, a question list for the next visit, and official recruiting US trials that open to the underlying record. Clinical Compass starts after diagnosis, while Ada, K Health, and Buoy focus on symptom guidance before diagnosis. I also chose not to manufacture an IQVIA-style prescribing ranking because I do not have the license or data rights.
Architecture

Two parallel waves, five single-purpose agents

Cards on

Five narrow workers answer five patient questions. Wave 2 waits for a verified drug list, and every cited number passes a source check before it reaches the page.

Why it matters: when evidence fails, the page shows a labeled gap instead of a polished guess.
openFDA labelopenFDA FAERSDailyMed PubMedClinicalTrials.govNICEMedlinePlus
Why these sources: FDA, openFDA, and DailyMed are official label records for warnings and adverse reactions. Named public guidelines provide treatment context. PubMed supplies published findings with study context. FAERS is only a secondary signal, never an incidence rate. ClinicalTrials.gov is the official registry for the recruiting-study links. The language model organizes and translates supplied evidence, but it is never the source of a clinical fact.
The boss agent normalizes the patient’s wording, then Wave 1 runs overview, standard of care, and trials in parallel. The verified drug list is the dependency gate for Wave 2, which handles label safety and alternatives. The validator checks the cited URL, quote, and number. Public sources were selected for accountability: FDA and DailyMed for labels, named guidelines for treatment context, PubMed for published findings, FAERS only for signals, and ClinicalTrials.gov for official trial records.
Demo, rheumatoid arthritis, steps 1 and 2

First, give the patient a foothold

The patient starts with a readable foothold, then chooses whether to inspect the source. Understanding comes before treatment evidence.

What this screen accomplishes: plain-language orientation, visible sources, and an optional privacy-preserving public-good signal.

Anonymous by design: one daily aggregate count per condition, with no account, IP address, or search history.
The landing screen accepts the disease name as a patient heard it, including abbreviations and alternate spelling. The checkbox is optional and unchecked by default. If enabled, the backend records only one aggregate count per canonical condition per day. That signal can guide translations, accessibility, clinician review, and outreach without becoming an advertising, insurance, or individual-care dataset.
Demo, rheumatoid arthritis, steps 3 and 4

The safest answer can be “not verified”

The validator caught an unsupported discontinuation-rate claim and removed it before it reached the patient page. The enlarged screenshot shows the safety failure and the source-backed evidence together.

Why this matters: an invented number can make a medicine look safer or more effective than the evidence supports. The safer answer is a visible gap.

Enlarged safety view: the boxed warning and amber validator message are readable at presentation size: the unsupported discontinuation-rate and published-trial claims were removed before display.

This is the strongest safety demonstration. The model generated a discontinuation-rate claim, but the source validator could not find a matching passage. The system removed it and displayed an honest gap. The supported ACR20 figure remains attached to its FDA label evidence. The clinician still interprets whether any treatment fits this individual patient.
Demo, rheumatoid arthritis, steps 5 through 7

From understanding to a better next conversation

The output is meant to leave the screen and enter the next appointment: three doctor questions plus a short list of recruiting US trials.

The patient leaves with agency: the cropped screens show the three-question agenda and one official trial card.

Every US trial card is clickable. The link opens the official ClinicalTrials.gov record, where the patient can inspect the sponsor, locations, eligibility, recruitment status, and contacts.
The questions are deliberately not treatment instructions. They help the patient ask about fit, expected benefit, monitoring, and warning signs. The trial worker filters for US locations, recruiting status, Phase 2 or later, and planned enrollment of at least 100. Each card opens the underlying ClinicalTrials.gov record. Clinical Compass surfaces candidates; the study team confirms eligibility and availability.

  • Prompt injection: retrieved pages pass to the model as untrusted data, never as instructions.
  • Unsupported claims: every quote and number is checked against its source before it's shown, or it's dropped.
Scale figures assume one lookup per user per month; per-run dollars are derived from published model rates, not Portkey invoice rows. The Portkey Analytics screenshot shows $7.22 and 209.6M tokens over an unfiltered 14-day window, plus 3.1K requests and 2,089 ms P50 latency. Those aggregate metrics confirm real activity but cannot be split by run. Type 2 diabetes used about 3.3 times the rheumatoid arthritis input tokens because of a larger evidence context and one validation retry. No uncapped baseline was run, so the quality check is observed evidence, not proof every optimization is harmless. The three measured runs show bounded usage, not an invoice: the configured key exposed token totals but not cached-input detail or billed dollars. The rate limit returned HTTP 429 on request seven, while the two-request extraction cap and source validator target overspending and unsupported claims.
Impact · reach, trust, and public-good data

The opportunity is serious. Early feedback is positive.

2×
more likely to be hospitalized at least once with inadequate vs. adequate health literacy in one cohortWilliams et al., 1998
31% lower
projected cost for patients who sustained high activation in their own care vs. low activationFairview / Health Affairs, 2015
Informal tester: “This is really cool and super easy to use. I like that it gives me clear information and questions to bring to my doctor instead of making me search through a bunch of medical websites.”
Reach scenarioStart with a 100-lookup pilot, then test a 10,000-lookup scale case. These are planning targets, not current usage claims.
Data that helps peopleAnonymous daily condition counts can reveal unmet information demand and prioritize new disease pages, translations, accessibility, and outreach.
Patient outcomeMeasure time to produce three concrete questions and confidence in the tradeoffs, not whether the tool made the treatment choice.
The two research figures establish the opportunity, not causation by Clinical Compass. Informal testers gave positive feedback; this is qualitative, not an outcome study. Impact hypothesis: if a patient recognizes a warning sign sooner, understands a treatment tradeoff, or stays engaged with a plan they and their clinician chose together, the result could be life-changing. A formal study should time one person creating three doctor questions without the app, then with it, and collect a consented quote. Anonymous daily counts can also show which conditions need new pages, translations, accessibility work, or outreach. The current evidence is qualitative and is labeled that way.
Where this goes

The hard part is already working

The evidence-first pipeline already works. Next: prove it helps patients use the next visit better.

Free to hospitals and patients. Paid later only on measured outcomes, never by selling patient data.

Next: a timed, consent-based user test and a clinician-reviewed pilot.
This started as a class project, but the evidence-first pipeline underneath it, guideline-driven, source-verified, and honest when it does not know, is the foundation any patient-facing health product would need. The first market is narrow on purpose: the moment after a serious, newly delivered diagnosis. The long-term ambition is a free, mobile-friendly public resource across conditions, languages, and reading levels. This is a focused distribution strategy: free to hospitals, broad public access, and value-based contracts only after measurable benefit is demonstrated. The product does not sell patient search history or let sponsors change treatment ordering. The first 90 days should turn positive user response into documented task timing, confidence change, and clinician review.
